title: Mastering Boolean Logic & Truth Tables 📊
description: Deep dive into `and`, `or`, `not`, truthiness, and short‑circuit evaluation for bulletproof conditions.

slides.title: Logic is the Glue of Hacking
slides.content:
# Every Decision Relies on Booleans

To build reliable tools, you must understand how `and`, `or`, and `not` really work – including truth tables and short‑circuiting. This lesson makes you a logic wizard.

slides.title: Truth Table for `and`
slides.content:
# Both Must Be True

| A     | B     | A and B |
|-------|-------|--------|
| True  | True  | True   |
| True  | False | False  |
| False | True  | False  |
| False | False | False  |

```python
if (port == 80) and (protocol == "HTTP"):
    ...
```

slides.title: Truth Table for `or`
slides.content:
# At Least One True

| A     | B     | A or B |
|-------|-------|--------|
| True  | True  | True   |
| True  | False | True   |
| False | True  | True   |
| False | False | False  |

```python
if (port == 80) or (port == 443):
    print("Web server")
```

quizData.question: What is `True or False`?
quizData.explanation: `or` needs only one True to return True.

slides.title: `not` – The Flipper
slides.content:
# Reverse the Boolean

| A     | not A |
|-------|-------|
| True  | False |
| False | True  |

```python
is_closed = False
if not is_closed:
    print("Port is open!")
```

slides.title: Complex Condition Example
slides.content: Check if a service is web‑related AND running on standard ports:
slides.codeSnippet:
service = "Apache"
port = 80
if (service in ["Apache", "nginx", "IIS"]) and (port == 80 or port == 443):
    print("Standard web server")

quizData.question: Evaluate: `(True and False) or (True and True)`

slides.title: Short‑Circuit Evaluation ⚡
slides.content:
# Python Stops As Soon As It Knows

* **`and`**: if the left side is False, the whole expression is False, so it **doesn't evaluate the right side**.
* **`or`**: if the left side is True, the whole expression is True, so it skips the right side.

This can improve performance and avoid errors:
```python
if (len(targets) > 0) and (targets[0] == "127.0.0.1"):
    ...
```
If `targets` is empty, `targets[0]` would cause IndexError, but short‑circuiting prevents it from being evaluated.

slides.title: Short‑Circuit in Practice

quizData.question: In `a or b`, if `a` is True, `b` is still evaluated.
quizData.explanation: `or` short‑circuits on True, so `b` is skipped.

slides.title: Truthiness – Non‑Bools in Conditions
slides.content:
# Every Object Has a Truth Value

Recall:
* **Falsy**: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `None`, `False`
* **Truthy**: everything else

You can leverage this:
```python
username = input("User: ")
if not username:
    print("No username entered")
```
This is equivalent to `if username == "":` but more Pythonic.

quizData.explanation: Empty list is falsy; space and non‑empty string are truthy.

slides.title: Parentheses for Clarity
slides.content:
# When in Doubt, Group

```python
if (port == 80 or port == 443) and (not blocked):
    ...
```
Without parentheses, `and` has higher precedence than `or`, which could change meaning. Use parentheses to make intent crystal clear.

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Use De Morgan's Laws to Simplify

`not (A and B)` is `(not A) or (not B)`  
`not (A or B)` is `(not A) and (not B)`

This can make some negative conditions more readable.
